title: COVID-19 vaccine misinformation in English-language news media: retrospective cohort study
screen_reason: Retrospective cohort of 1,298,054 English-language COVID-19 vaccine articles published 27 July 2020 - 30 June 2021 by the 100 online news outlets with the greatest reach (Cision NextGen). A Boolean misinformation string flagged 41,718 articles (3.2%), and a close read of a random 500 of those by two trained coders separated primary misinformation from fact-checking and mere reference, yielding the paper's headline prevalence: approximately 0.096% (95% CI 0.05-0.16%) of all COVID-19 vaccine articles contained primary misinformation. Item-level shares of articles judged against a coding rubric, with denominators, so CONTENT.

estimates.country: English-language outlets, multiple countries; among the misinformation-flagged articles the country of origin was the USA (60%), UK (9%), Canada (7%), India (5%) and Australia (4%); the underlying database also draws on Ireland and New Zealand
estimates.platform: Online traditional news media (professionally generated content from the 100 highest-reach English-language news outlets and news-focused blogs), aggregated by Cision NextGen Communications Cloud including licensed print/traditional media via LexisNexis; social media excluded
estimates.date: 27 July 2020 (start of Moderna and Pfizer phase 3 trials) - 30 June 2021; the close-read subset was drawn from 27 July 2020 - 19 January 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of all COVID-19 vaccine news articles that contained PRIMARY misinformation (articles promoting misinformation), estimated by applying the close-read primary-misinformation rate to the Boolean-flagged share
estimates.value_raw: 0.096% (3.2% x 3.0%; 95% CI 0.05% to 0.16%); reported in the Abstract and Discussion as 'approximately 0.1%'. A sensitivity estimate removing the 65 articles that were unavailable or paywalled gives 0.11% (95% CI 0.06% to 0.18%)
estimates.denominator: 1,298,054 English-language articles on COVID-19 vaccines published 27 July 2020 - 30 June 2021 in the 100 online news outlets and news-focused blogs with the greatest reach (themselves 4.8% of the 27,122,380 COVID-19 vaccine articles the Boolean string found across the whole database)
estimates.definition: Article coded 'primary misinformation', defined as an article PROMOTING misinformation - as distinct from 'fact-checking' (articles concerned with determining whether certain assertions were accurate) and 'refers to misinformation' (made reference to misinformation but did not advance it). Misinformation content was defined by 17 subthemes grouped into six themes (safety; development, production and distribution; conspiracies; morality and ethics; political and financial; alternative treatments)
estimates.misinfo_def: Operationalised through 17 subthemes with explicit definitions, e.g. 'Cause death: False claims that COVID vaccines cause death rather than prevent infection'; 'DNA/RNA alteration: Claims that COVID-19 vaccines alter DNA, usually referencing novel RNA processes'; 'Microchips: General theories about microchip implantation via COVID-19 vaccines'; 'Miracle cures: Unfounded claims that various alternative remedies such as hydroxychloroquine or colloidal silver are preferable to vaccines'. Article-level categories: 'primary misinformation (ie, articles promoting misinformation)'

estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 6 (full sentence quoted in rob.item10_quote); Abstract gives 'approximately 0.1% (95% CI 0.05% to 0.16%)'; Discussion p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two-stage. (1) A Boolean string built from 17 subthemes derived from materials of three vaccine-focused organisations (Planned Parenthood, the Adult Vaccine Access Coalition, the Immunisation Action Coalition) plus Google searches, iteratively refined against 20 randomly selected articles per subtheme; sensitivity checked against 50 articles known to contain misinformation, 49/50 (98%) retrieved, i.e. a low false-negative rate. (2) Close read of 500 randomly selected flagged articles (highest random-ID method) against a predetermined coding rubric: 200 read by TWO coders, the remaining 300 by one of the two, with an author (JA) resolving disagreements and refining practice. No kappa or percent-agreement statistic is reported. The authors acknowledge the Boolean string had 'a fairly high false-positive rate' (31.6% of flagged articles were unrelated) and that close readings 'are by their nature subjective'.
estimates.moderator_quote: Articles were characterised as either (1) primary misinformation (ie, articles promoting misinformation); (2) fact-checking (ie, articles concerned with determining whether certain assertions were accurate) or (3) refers to misinformation (ie, made reference to misinformation but did not advance it or referenced the COVID-19 vaccine 'infodemic' without providing specific fact-checking).
estimates.notes: This is the row to use for prevalence: it is the paper's headline conclusion ('COVID-19 vaccine misinformation in traditional media is uncommon'). Three caveats for an adjudicator. (1) It is a two-stage product (Boolean-flagged share x close-read primary-misinformation rate), stated verbatim by the authors with a Clopper-Pearson CI, so it satisfies R8, but it is not a directly observed count. (2) denom_selection=curated because the denominator is restricted to the 100 highest-reach outlets - a rank-truncated set; the authors state they cannot generalise beyond these outlets or to non-English sources. (3) The close-read subset covers only 27 July 2020 - 19 January 2021, so the primary-misinformation rate from the first half of the study period is applied to the full year; the authors defend this with the stability of the misinformation percentage after October 2020. year=2021 is the midpoint-and-modal year of the 27 Jul 2020 - 30 Jun 2021 window (article volume roughly tripled after November 2020). source_quote is a short exact fragment because the paper is set in two interleaved columns, so the full sentence is not a contiguous span in the extracted text; the complete sentence is preserved verbatim in rob.item10_quote and in value_raw.

estimates.country: English-language outlets, multiple countries (USA 60%, UK 9%, Canada 7%, India 5%, Australia 4% among the flagged articles)
estimates.platform: Online traditional news media (100 highest-reach English-language outlets), Cision NextGen
estimates.measure_type: % of all COVID-19 vaccine news articles flagged by the automated Boolean string as containing at least one vaccine misinformation theme (broad, unvalidated definition - includes fact-checking and mere mentions)
estimates.value_raw: 41,718/1,298,054 (3.2%) [exact 3.21%]; themes within the flagged set: safety 23,448 (56.2%), development/production/distribution 11,114 (26.6%), conspiracies 6,289 (15.1%), morality and ethics 1,806 (4.3%), political and financial 1,731 (4.1%), alternative treatments 771 (1.8%)
estimates.denominator: 1,298,054 English-language COVID-19 vaccine articles from the 100 highest-reach outlets, 27 July 2020 - 30 June 2021
estimates.definition: Article matched by the study's Boolean search string for at least one of six vaccine misinformation themes (17 subthemes). The match does NOT establish that the article advanced the misinformation: on close read, 31.6% of flagged articles were unrelated, 63.2% of the confirmed ones were fact-checking and 31.4% merely referred to misinformation
estimates.misinfo_def: Same 17 subtheme definitions as the strict row, e.g. 'Developed too quickly: Discourse around unverified claims that the development process was rushed'; 'Population control: Theories that COVID vaccines will be used for population control'
estimates.source_quote: Articles containing misinformation from 100 outlets with greatest reach 41 718 (3.2%)
estimates.page_loc: Table 2 'Summary of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation findings', p. 6; also Results p. 3 and the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Automated Boolean keyword string over the Cision NextGen database, built from 17 subthemes and iteratively refined on 20 randomly drawn articles per subtheme. Sensitivity: 49/50 (98%) of articles known to contain misinformation were retrieved (low false-negative rate). Precision: poor - of 500 flagged articles close-read, 158 (31.6%) were unrelated to vaccine misinformation, often because of sidebar advertisements or links to other articles, and 65 (13.0%) were unavailable.
estimates.moderator_quote: Articles associated with each subtheme were generated by Boolean strings. For each subtheme, we randomly selected 20 articles and refined the Boolean string in iterative fashion until all articles not consistent with that subtheme were eliminated. ... To establish the sensitivity of this approach, we identified 50 articles known to contain misinformation; 49 of these (98%) were identified by the search string.
estimates.notes: borderline=true and definition_variant=true: 3.2% is the number most likely to be misread as the prevalence of vaccine misinformation in the news, and it is not. It is a keyword match on misinformation THEMES, and the paper's own validation shows the flagged set is dominated by fact-checking (63.2% of confirmed articles) and passing reference (31.4%), with only 5.4% primary misinformation; a third of flagged articles were not about vaccine misinformation at all. It is recorded because it is the abstract's headline count and because a broad 'mentions misinformation' definition is a genuine definition variant of the same country x platform cell, but it must never be pooled as a prevalence of false content. The strict 0.096% row is the correct prevalence estimate from this paper.

estimates.platform: Online traditional news media (100 highest-reach English-language outlets), Cision NextGen
estimates.measure_type: % of close-read Boolean-flagged COVID-19 vaccine articles confirmed to contain a misinformation theme that were PRIMARY misinformation (articles promoting misinformation) rather than fact-checking or mere reference
estimates.value_raw: 15/277 (5.4%) primary misinformation, against fact-checking 175/277 (63.2%) and refers-to-misinformation 87/277 (31.4%); equivalently 15/500 (3.0%; 95% CI 1.7% to 4.9%) of all randomly selected Boolean-flagged articles
estimates.denominator: 277 close-read articles confirmed to contain at least one misinformation theme, out of 500 randomly selected from those identified by the Boolean misinformation string in the period 27 July 2020 - 19 January 2021 (158 of the 500 were unrelated and 65 unavailable/paywalled)
estimates.definition: Article coded 'primary misinformation' (promoting misinformation) by trained coders using a predetermined rubric, as opposed to fact-checking or merely referring to misinformation
estimates.page_loc: Table 2, 'Categories in close-read subset (N=277)', p. 6; Results p. 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 500 articles selected by inserting a random unique identifier into each record and taking the 500 highest; 200 of these read independently by two coders following a predetermined rubric, the remaining 300 by one of the two; author JA resolved disagreements and refined coding practice. No inter-coder reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: To determine whether the articles identified by the Boolean misinformation string really contained misinformation and to examine those that did in greater detail, we randomly selected 500 articles from the period 27 July 2020 to 19 January 2021.
estimates.notes: within_misinfo_content=true per R3: the denominator is a misinformation-flagged sample, not a natural corpus, so this belongs in the appendix and never in a prevalence pool. It is recorded because it is the validation step that turns the broad 3.2% into the strict 0.096%, and because the composition it reveals - most flagged coverage is fact-checking (63.2%), not misinformation - is substantively important. The equivalent figure on the full 500-article random subset is 3.0% (95% CI 1.7% to 4.9%), which is the multiplier the authors actually used. year=2020 for this row because the close-read window is 27 July 2020 - 19 January 2021, mostly 2020. source_quote is the Table 2 cell, the only contiguous verbatim rendering (the paper is set in two interleaved columns).

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted. (a) REACH-like figures: 'In eight study weeks, the reach of these 277 articles (defined as visitors to the sites containing the articles) exceeded 250 million people', weekly peaks of 300-450 million unique visitors, 'Fact-checking accounted for 69.6% of all reach', 'Primary misinformation represented 5.5% of all reach', and the country splits of reach (USA 80.8%, UK 10.8%, India 2.8%; primary-misinformation reach share UK 15.6% vs USA 8.9%). These are absolute site-visitor counts and shares of reach WITHIN the 277-article subset, not a share of people who encountered misinformation at least once out of a defined population, so they do not meet the review's REACH definition; the authors themselves warn 'there is no assurance that visitors actually read the articles in question' and that reach is desktop-only. (b) Theme composition of the 41,718 flagged articles (safety 56.2%, development 26.6%, conspiracies 15.1%, morality/ethics 4.3%, political/financial 4.1%, alternatives 1.8%) and of the 277 close-read articles (development 54.5%, safety 44.8%, conspiracies 24.2%, etc.), plus subtheme counts (general side effects 23.2%, developed too quickly 13.3%) - all within-misinformation composition, not prevalence, and non-mutually-exclusive so they sum above 100%. (c) '277/500 (55.4%) contained at least one misinformation theme' - a precision statistic for the Boolean string. (d) The 0.11% sensitivity estimate excluding the 65 unavailable/paywalled articles is recorded in value_raw of the strict row rather than as a fourth row (R4). (e) '1,298,054 articles ... (4.8%)' of the 27,122,380 total vaccine articles is an outlet-coverage share, not a misinformation share. (f) Figures quoted from other studies (409 anti-vaccination accounts with 58 million followers; 28% believing vaccines contain microchips in Arab countries; 1.1 million COVID misinformation articles in the authors' earlier study; UK vaccine hesitancy 39% to 11%; Japanese HPV uptake 80% to under 1%) are cited from elsewhere and barred by R8.

rob.design: Retrospective cohort of online news content. Source: Cision NextGen Communications Cloud, a commercial aggregator spanning over 7 million global print, broadcast and online sources (including licensed print/traditional media via LexisNexis), excluding social media; restricted to English. Window 27 July 2020 (start of Moderna/Pfizer phase 3 trials) - 30 June 2021. A Boolean string for COVID-19 vaccine articles returned 27,122,380 articles; the study was then restricted to the 100 outlets with the greatest reach, identified by taking the 10,000 highest-reach articles on the 15th and 16th of the middle month of each quarter of 2020 (5,815 unique outlets), ranking by Similarweb desktop unique-visitor reach for calendar 2020, and excluding non-news sites (e.g. Good Housekeeping, weather.com, Psychology Today) by consensus of six authors, replacing each with the next highest-reach outlet. This yielded 1,298,054 vaccine articles (4.8% of all found). Misinformation identification: 17 subthemes drawn from three vaccine organisations' public materials plus Google searches, grouped into six themes, each operationalised as a Boolean string refined iteratively against 20 random articles per subtheme; sensitivity 49/50 (98%) on articles known to contain misinformation. Validation: 500 articles randomly selected (random unique identifier, top 500) from 27 July 2020 - 19 January 2021; 200 double-coded by two coders against a predetermined rubric, 300 single-coded, disagreements resolved by author JA; articles classified as primary misinformation, fact-checking, or refers-to-misinformation, and tagged non-mutually-exclusively to themes/subthemes. 95% CIs by Clopper-Pearson. No inter-coder reliability statistic reported. Stated limitations: automated approach yields false positives (31.6% of flagged articles unrelated); close reads are subjective; no generalisation beyond the top 100 outlets or to non-English sources; reach is desktop-only and does not prove readership; rarity of primary misinformation precluded cross-tabulation by outlet and country. Funding: none declared for this study; competing interests note Cision's commercial media-analysis business and Alliance for Science funding from the Gates Foundation. No patient/public involvement; not human-subjects research.
rob.item6_quote: Articles were characterised as either (1) primary misinformation (ie, articles promoting misinformation); (2) fact-checking (ie, articles concerned with determining whether certain assertions were accurate) or (3) refers to misinformation (ie, made reference to misinformation but did not advance it or referenced the COVID-19 vaccine 'infodemic' without providing specific fact-checking).
rob.item10_quote: Overall, of 1 298 054 articles on COVID-19 vaccines, 3.2% contained apparent misinformation according to our search string and 15 articles in our random subset of 500 (3.0%; 95% CI 1.7% to 4.9%) contained primary misinformation. Thus, one can estimate that 0.096% of all COVID-19 vaccine articles (3.2%*3.0%; 95% CI 0.05% to 0.16%) contained primary misinformation.
